newsitem.title: GREECE: FOCUS - Greek FRNs have more room on the upside - bankers.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Greek FRNs have more room on the upside - bankers.

text.p: The bull run of Greek floaters has farther to go on expectations of fresh spread cuts, lower inflation, interbank rates and selling commissions that will propel them to new highs, bankers said.

"I believe FRNs will continue to rally although at a slower speed," said George Georgiou, general manager at Bayerische Vereinsbank, Athens. "Prospects for lower inflation, interest rates, cuts in FRN spreads, commissions provide a solid launch pad."
Consumer price inflation fell to 6.8 percent year-on-year in January from 7.3 percent in December and is expected to settle lower, around 6.5 percent in February.
The gross yield on the 12-month T-bill, the reference rate for FRNs, was set at 10.50 percent for the end-February issue from 10.90 percent at end-January.
Seven-year conventional FRNs are the debt instrument auctioned consistently for more than a year by the finance ministry.
It is the only Greek interest rate instrument that foreign banks have written options on.

"I am bullish about Greek debt instruments in general and FRNs in particular," said Nikos Sikiarides, treasurer at Barclays bank PLC, Athens. "A host of factors such as prospects for lower inflation and interest rates this year provide a safety valve."
Other bankers agreed that fresh spread cuts would boost FRN prices but they pointed out that only cuts bigger than 50 basis points would have a positive effect on bond valuations.

"FRN spreads are way behind the curve," said Harris Makkas, country treasurer at Bank of America, Athens. "Even if they were to be slashed by 50 basis points they would simply validate existing market valuations."
The current FRN spreads stand at 130 basis points in the primary market but have receded to about 70 basis points in the secondary bond market.

Bankers also stressed that non-residents domiciled in countries having a double taxation treaty with Greece, faced a positive carry with FRNs, unlike some other state securities such as three-year coupon bonds. This improved the appeal of floaters.

"Non-residents can fund FRNs through forex forwards in one-year tenors at around 10.50 percent which is lower than the yield to first-coupon when selling commissions and a negligible tax impact is expected," said a senior dealer at a foreign bank.

In addition to the positive carry, Moody's recent upgrading of Greek foreign currency-denominated and drachma-denominated debt made non-residents more comfortable with Greek domestic debt, giving a helping hand to FRNs, bankers said.
But funding through depos is less attractive with one-year rates around 11.30 percent and short-term rates supported by the the central bank's 11.90 percent overnight intervention bid.

"If one expects interbank depo rates to decline and the central bank to cut its overnight intervention rate sharply, then he can trade the current negative carry against capital gains and much lower rates in the future," the dealer said.

The finance ministry is paying banks a gross selling commission ranging from 0.45 percent on 12-month T-bills to 1.10 percent on seven-year FRNs. Most local banks pass on all or a big chunk of it to their big clients.
A withholding tax of 7.5 percent was levied on interest income from treasuries issued from January 1 but capital gains are not taxed. Securities issued prior to 1997 were not taxed.

A finance ministry circular obtained by Reuters said that non-residents from countries having a double taxation treaty with Greece would get a tax rebate within 30 days from the day they submitted their tax refund application.
But finance ministry officials told Reuters that the final draft was not out yet and cautioned against drawing premature conclusions.
Mutual funds and investment companies are taxed at 0.2 percent on their net assets. The tax regime for local banks, corporations and non-residents has yet to be clarified.

The different tax treatment of securities has created a wedge in yields between tax-free and taxable securities that mirrors uncertainty about the tax rebate for non-residents domiciled in countries having a double taxation treaty with Greece.
"The wedge reflects uncertainty about the recovery of taxes paid by non-residents," said Makkas. "It will likely shrink and stabilise when the pertaining tax issues are clarified by the ministry."
Bankers were also quick to point out that FRNs were more attractive relative to other debt instruments in terms of annual yields for retail investors who used to buy 12-month T-bills in the past.

But they warned against possible downward risks if the finance ministry proceeded with sizable interest rate cuts on the reference 12-month T-bill that would turn off investors' desire for these instruments.
"The basis risk is definitely a big minus for FRNs," said another senior foreign bank dealer.
He was referring to the finance ministry's tendency to set the interest rates on the reference 12-month T-bill administratively instead of auctioning the security.

Other factors that could breathe life into the nearly three-month old FRN rally were the likelihood of a reduced supply in 1997 on the back of a smaller public sector borrowing requirement (PSBR) and the ample liquidity of fixed income funds.

"If the finance ministry decides to slim this year's supply of FRNs or even cease auctioning the instrument, this would boost the prices of outstanding FRNs," said the treasurer of Bayerische Vereinsbank.
